implementation_notes: C has no heap in the standard library, so the structure is the array plus the two sift routines, with the element type as a void* plus a comparator or as a fixed-size element. For C the right practical advice is usually to write a small, well-tested generic heap once (sift-up, sift-down, heapify) rather than to reach for qsort at each call site - qsort cannot maintain an incremental heap and its comparator cannot report a stable tie order. If the priority key is a small integer, a bucket array is simpler and faster. Reserve capacity up front: realloc during a push invalidates nothing here (the array is owned) but costs the copy.
idiom_name: void*-element array plus comparator function pointer, with hand-written sift routines
pitfalls: The comparator must be a strict weak ordering; an inconsistent comparator makes sift-up and sift-down disagree about the root and the failure is silent.
Struct assignment per level is the cost - hole-punching (move the value once at the end) is what makes this cheap for non-trivial types.
The array reallocates on push; for a latency-sensitive queue, reserve capacity up front.
qsort is not a heap: it sorts, and it cannot maintain an incrementally updated heap, so it is the wrong tool for a scheduler.
